name: WISP
tagline: A commercial game server management panel that hosting companies resell to their customers.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: WISP is built for people selling game servers to strangers: multi-tenant accounts, subuser permissions, SFTP, billing hooks, node fleets. If all you want is to run your own Minecraft, Valheim and Rust servers on one box, most of that is dead weight. An agent can absolutely produce a single-user panel that starts, stops and consoles dockerized game servers in a sitting, and Pterodactyl already exists for free if you want the full thing. The gaps show up at the edges: the curated per-game install and startup configs, a real file manager, SFTP, scheduled backups and multi-node orchestration each cost you another day. So it is a yes for your own hardware and a no if you were planning to resell.
coreLoopDIY: A local web panel that launches each of your game servers as a Docker container with resource limits, streams the console over a websocket, and lets you send commands, restart, and snapshot the data volume.
requirements: A Linux box or VM you control with Docker installed
Ports you are willing to expose, and a firewall you actually configured
Per-game knowledge of image, startup command and volume layout
whatYouLose: The curated library of per-game install scripts and startup variables, which is the part that quietly eats your weekends
Multi-tenant accounts, subusers and granular permissions, so no handing a server to a friend without handing over everything
SFTP access, a proper in-browser file manager and editor
Scheduled tasks, backups and multi-node allocation management
Someone to blame and a support queue when a game update breaks the startup flags
moatNotes: The real product is the long tail of game configs plus the reseller plumbing, not the start/stop button.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for WISP because they are running a business, not a basement server. Once you have paying customers you need account isolation, subuser roles, SFTP, billing integration, per-node allocations and a panel that does not embarrass you when a fourteen year old opens it. Keeping up with dozens of game servers as each one changes its launch arguments is a maintenance treadmill, and outsourcing that treadmill is the whole value. If you are an audience of one, none of that applies.
notes: Check whether Pterodactyl already does everything you need before you write a line of this.
prompt:
Build a single-user, self-hosted game server control panel called "emberpanel". Local network use only, no accounts system, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Node 22 with TypeScript, Express, and the ws package
- dockerode to talk to the local Docker socket
- better-sqlite3 for state, file at ./data/panel.db
- Server-rendered EJS pages plus xterm.js loaded from a local vendored file for the console
- No React, no build step beyond tsc

Functionality in scope:
- A servers.yaml file at the repo root defines each game server: id, display name, docker image, env vars, exposed ports, volume path under ./volumes/{id}, memory limit, cpu limit, stop command
- On boot, reconcile servers.yaml into SQLite; do not auto-start anything
- Dashboard listing each server with state (running, stopped, unhealthy), uptime, and live CPU and memory from the Docker stats stream
- Per-server page with start, stop, restart, and kill buttons
- Live console: stream container stdout over a websocket into xterm.js, and send typed lines back into the container stdin
- Graceful stop sends the configured stop command to stdin, waits 30 seconds, then kills
- Backups: tar the server volume into ./backups/{id}/{timestamp}.tar.gz on demand, list them, delete them, restore one while the server is stopped
- Single shared password from PANEL_PASSWORD in .env, session cookie, all routes behind it

Explicitly out of scope: multi-user accounts, subusers, SFTP, a file manager, multi-node support, billing, scheduled tasks, HTTPS termination.

Deliver a .env.example with PANEL_PASSWORD and PANEL_PORT, a servers.yaml with working Minecraft and Valheim examples, npm scripts for dev and start, and a README that states plainly that this panel must not be exposed to the public internet.
